content: Interactions were found to be associated with accelerated wound healing. Researchers proposed that this effect might be due to oxytocin's ability to reduce inflammation, thereby facilitating faster wound repair. This study offers preliminary evidence suggesting that positive social interactions can directly influence certain aspects of health. A 2014 study demonstrated that silencing oxytocin receptors in interneurons within the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) of female mice led to a loss of social interest in male mice during the sexually receptive phase of the estrous cycle. Oxytocin has been shown to elicit feelings of contentment, reduce anxiety, and promote a sense of calmness and security, particularly in the presence of a mate. This indicates that oxytocin may play a critical role in inhibiting brain regions associated with behavioral control, fear, and anxiety, thereby enabling the occurrence of orgasm. Research has also shown that oxytocin can reduce anxiety and provide protection against stress, especially when combined with social support. Additionally, it has been discovered that endocannabinoid signaling mediates oxytocin-driven social reward. Oxytocin is a peptide hormone composed of nine amino acids (a nonapeptide) with the sequence cysteine-tyrosine-isoleucine-glutamine-asparagine-cysteine-proline-leucine-glycine-amide (Cys-Tyr-Ile-Gln-Asn-Cys-Pro-Leu-Gly-NH2, or CYIQNCPLG-NH2). Its C-terminus is modified into a primary amide, and a disulfide bridge links the cysteine residues. The structure of oxytocin is highly conserved among placental mammals. However, a novel structure of oxytocin has been identified in certain New World primates, such as marmosets and tamarins. Genomic sequencing of the oxytocin gene revealed a single in-frame mutation (thymine replacing cytosine), resulting in an amino acid substitution at position 8 (proline replacing leucine). Since the original findings by Lee et al., two additional laboratories have confirmed the presence of Pro8-OT and documented other structural variants of oxytocin in this primate group. Vargas-Pinilla et al. sequenced the coding regions of the OXT gene in other New World primates and identified additional variants, including Ala8-OT, Thr8-OT, and Val3/Pro8-OT. Ren et al. further identified a variant, Phe2-OT, in howler monkeys. The biologically active form of oxytocin, commonly measured using radioimmunoassay (RIA) or high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC), is known as the octapeptide oxytocin disulfide (oxidized form). However, oxytocin also exists in a reduced, linear (non-cyclic) dithiol form called oxytoceine. It has been hypothesized that oxytoceine may act as a free radical scavenger, donating an electron to neutralize free radicals and subsequently being re-oxidized to oxytocin via the dehydroascorbate/ascorbate redox couple. The structure of oxytocin closely resembles that of vasopressin. Both are nonapeptides with a single disulfide bridge, differing only by two amino acid substitutions in their sequences. Vasopressin's sequence is Cys-Tyr-Phe-Gln-Asn-Cys-Pro-Arg-Gly-NH2, with the differences from oxytocin highlighted for clarity. Oxytocin and vasopressin were first isolated and synthesized in 1954, a groundbreaking achievement for which Vincent du Vigneaud was awarded the 1955 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. These two hormones are the only known hormones released by the human posterior pituitary gland that act at distant sites. However, oxytocin neurons also produce other peptides, such as corticotropin-releasing hormone and dynorphin, which act locally. The magnocellular neurosecretory cells that produce oxytocin are located adjacent to those that produce vasopressin. These are large neuroendocrine neurons capable of generating action potentials. The uterine-contracting properties of the substance later named oxytocin were first discovered by British pharmacologist Sir Henry Hallett Dale in 1906. Its role in milk ejection was described by Ott and Scott in 1910 and by Schafer and Mackenzie in 1911. In the 1920s, oxytocin and vasopressin were isolated from pituitary tissue and given their current names. The term oxytocin was derived from the Greek words oxys (sharp or quick) and toketos (birth), meaning quick birth. Oxytocin was the first polypeptide hormone to be sequenced and synthesized, a milestone that earned du Vigneaud the Nobel Prize in 1955.
